Baccarat Basics: Banker, Player, Tie, and Why the Banker Bet Is the Play

Published August 26, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Baccarat has a reputation as an intimidating, high-roller-only game, which is strange given that it's one of the simplest games on the floor once you strip away the ceremony. There are only three bets, no strategy decisions to memorize, and a fixed set of drawing rules that the dealer follows automatically. The only real decision a player makes all night is which of three boxes to put chips on — and one of those three is a meaningfully better bet than the other two.

  2. How a baccarat hand is scored

The three bets: banker, player, and tie

Every round of baccarat comes down to two hands, dealt from a shoe of six or eight decks and labeled "Player" and "Banker" — names that describe two positions in the game, not the dealer versus the casino. Before cards are dealt, everyone at the table bets on one of three outcomes: that the Player hand will finish closer to 9, that the Banker hand will finish closer to 9, or that the two hands will tie. Whichever hand you bet on doesn't require you to hold or touch any cards; the dealer deals both hands face up according to fixed rules, and every player at the table is simply betting on the result, the same as betting on a coin flip at a craps table rather than flipping the coin yourself.

How a baccarat hand is scored

Cards 2 through 9 count at face value, 10s and face cards count as zero, and aces count as one. When a hand's total goes above 9, only the last digit counts — a hand of 7 and 8 totals 15, which scores as 5. That single rule is the entire scoring system: no hand can ever be worth more than 9, and the closest hand to 9 wins the round. A two-card total of 8 or 9 is called a "natural," and it ends the round immediately with no further cards drawn by either hand.

Takeaway: You never have to do arithmetic under pressure at the table — the dealer totals both hands and the drawing rules are automatic. Your only job is choosing where to place a chip before the cards come out.

The drawing rules: why a third card is dealt automatically

If neither hand has a natural 8 or 9 after the first two cards, a fixed table of rules — printed on most physical layouts and built into every digital version — decides whether either hand draws a third card. The Player hand draws on a total of 0-5 and stands on 6 or 7. The Banker hand's third-card rule is more involved because it depends partly on whether the Player hand drew a card and, if so, what that card's value was — but critically, none of this requires a decision from anyone at the table. The rules exist purely to keep the house edge fixed and identical every time the game is played, which is part of why baccarat strategy guides are so short compared to blackjack's: there's genuinely nothing to decide.

House edge by bet, and why banker wins that comparison

Because the Banker hand gets a slight structural advantage from the third-card drawing rules — acting somewhat like a player who gets to see one more piece of information before deciding whether to draw — it wins more often than the Player hand over the long run. That's the entire reason the banker bet is considered the strongest wager in the game: it has a lower house edge than the player bet, and dramatically lower than the tie bet, purely as a mathematical consequence of the fixed drawing rules rather than any pattern or "streak" a table might be showing.

BetApproximate house edgeTypical payout
Banker~1.06%1:1, minus a 5% commission on wins
Player~1.24%1:1
Tie~14.4%8:1 or 9:1, depending on the table

That gap between roughly 1% and roughly 14% is enormous by casino standards — the tie bet is one of the worst-value single bets on the entire floor, despite the tempting double-digit payout, because ties happen far less often than the payout would need to occur to break even.

The 5% commission on banker wins

The catch with the banker bet is that a standard baccarat table charges a 5% commission on winning banker bets specifically, to offset the edge the bet would otherwise hand to the player. A $100 winning banker bet pays $95 rather than a full $100, and most physical tables track commission owed on a rack rather than collecting it after every single hand. Some newer table variants — often marketed as "commission-free baccarat" — remove the 5% charge but instead pay a reduced amount (commonly half the normal payout) when the Banker hand wins specifically with a total of 6, which is a different way of recovering roughly the same edge. Always check which version you're playing before assuming the numbers above apply exactly as written.

A worked hand from start to finish

Say the Player hand is dealt a 4 and a 3, totaling 7, and stands under the fixed drawing rule for any Player total of 6 or 7. The Banker hand is dealt a 2 and a 2, totaling 4. Because the Player stood rather than drawing a third card, the Banker's drawing rule at a total of 4 says to draw a card. The Banker draws a 5, bringing the total to 9 — a winning hand for anyone who bet Banker, since 9 beats the Player's 7. A $50 banker bet would pay $47.50 after the 5% commission; the same $50 bet on Player would have lost outright.

Common mistakes and myths

The most common myth in baccarat is scorecard tracking — many tables provide a printed card for players to mark which hand won each round, which feeds a widespread but false belief that recent results predict the next hand. Every round is dealt independently from a shuffled shoe; a Banker hand winning five times in a row has no bearing on the next round's odds. The second common mistake is betting the tie for its payout without weighing its much higher house edge — occasional ties do happen, but chasing that payout consistently costs far more over time than it returns. The simplest, mathematically best approach for most players is to bet Banker every hand and accept the modest commission, since it's the lowest house edge available at the table.

Baccarat's low house edge on the banker bet describes long-run averages, not a guarantee for any individual session. Set a loss limit before you sit down, and see our responsible gambling resources if betting ever stops feeling like entertainment.

Frequently asked questions

Is baccarat a game of skill or pure chance?

Pure chance. The drawing rules are fixed and automatic, so no decision a player makes during a hand affects the outcome — the only meaningful choice is which of the three bets to place before the cards are dealt.

Why does the banker bet charge a commission if it's the best bet?

The Banker hand's drawing rules give it a structural edge over the Player hand, so casinos charge a 5% commission on banker wins specifically to bring the house edge back in line — even after the commission, banker still edges out player.

Should I ever bet the tie?

Generally no. The tie bet's roughly 14% house edge is far higher than banker or player, and the payout doesn't come close to compensating for how rarely ties actually occur.

Does the number of decks in the shoe change the house edge much?

Slightly — house edge figures are typically quoted for an eight-deck shoe, and fewer decks shift the numbers by small fractions of a percent, not enough to change which bet is best.

Is "commission-free" baccarat actually better for players?

Not meaningfully — it typically pays a reduced amount when Banker wins with a total of 6 instead of charging the standard 5% commission, which recovers a similar house edge through a different mechanism.
